about: Building types (roadmap BT1c3a): health and welfare: hospitals, almshouses, asylums, poor relief, baths and wash-houses. Same fields as lineage.json.

types.name: Medieval hospital (hospitium, maison dieu)

period.text: from before the Norman Conquest; St Bartholomew's, London, founded 1123; in England the church ceased to support hospitals at the Dissolution (1540), while in Scotland hospitals, bedehouses and maisons Dieu were built from c. 1144 to c. 1650

types.note: FISH has no term of its own for the medieval hospital; HOSPITAL is its general term. A medieval hospital was a house of hospitality for the poor, travellers and the sick, not only a place of treatment.
types.plan: a large hall with beds along the walls, joined to a chapel and sometimes a kitchen; courtyard plans became more common in the later Middle Ages

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the medieval period, hospitals were places of hospitality, providing shelter and basic care rather than medical treatment alone.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In England, some of the earliest recorded hospitals date from before the Norman Conquest.

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: After the dissolution of the monasteries in 1540 by King Henry VIII the church abruptly ceased to be the supporter of hospitals, and only by direct petition from the citizens of London, were the hospitals St Bartholomew's, St Thomas's and St Mary of Bethlehem's (Bedlam) endowed directly by the crown.

sources.title: Hospitals in medieval Scotland
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From c. 1144 to c. 1650 many hospitals, bedehouses and maisons Dieu were built in Scotland.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Almshouses developed from monastic infirmaries, typically arranged as large halls with bed spaces along the walls and were connected to a chapel and, in some cases, a kitchen.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From the later medieval period, courtyard designs became more common, with individual living spaces arranged around a central courtyard, often entered through a gate or archway, and with a residence for the master incorporated into the gatehouse.

types.name: Leper hospital (lazar house)

period.text: Harbledown, founded by Lanfranc c. 1085, the first recorded; most founded in England between 1100 and 1250; no source here dates the last foundation: as leprosy declined some became almshouses, and it was nearly gone from Europe by 1700

types.plan: a church with separate shelters for the lepers

sources.title: Harbledown
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The leper's hospital was founded in 1085 by Archbishop Lanfranc; "the hospital and well can still be seen".

sources.title: History of leprosy
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first recorded leper colony was in Harbledown, England.

sources.title: History of leprosy
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The expansion of asylums in England between 1100 and 1250 was not necessarily in response to a major epidemic of leprosy.

sources.title: Leper colony
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Recent research has shown M. leprae has maintained a similarly virulent genome over at least the last thousand years, leaving it unclear which precise factors led to leprosy's near elimination in Europe by 1700.

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: Leper Hospital
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.

types.name: Voluntary hospital

period.text: from 1718 (the French Hospital, Finsbury; Westminster Hospital 1719, Guy's 1724); St Mary's (1851) the last of London's six great voluntary hospitals; taken over by the National Health Service in 1948

types.note: In FISH 'voluntary hospital' is a non-preferred term of GENERAL HOSPITAL; SUBSCRIPTION HOSPITAL is a separate term.

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first voluntary hospital created to provide free care through the philanthropic action of doctors and surgeons for the ill poor was the French Hospital in Finsbury, London, started in 1718 by Huguenot immigrants.

sources.title: Voluntary hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the middle of the 18th century, there were six in London: St Barts, Guy's, St Thomas', Westminster, St George's, and St Mary's (the last to be founded in England, in 1851).

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The National Health Service, the principal provider of health care in Britain, was founded in 1948, and took control of nearly all the hospitals.

period.text: the London Dispensary of 1696 the first; common from the 1770s (Edinburgh 1776, London 1779-80); rooms for giving out medicines are still part of hospitals and clinics; no source here dates the end of the charitable dispensary

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The idea was slow to catch on until the 1770s, when many such organizations began to appear, including the Public Dispensary of Edinburgh (1776), the Metropolitan Dispensary and Charitable Fund (1779) and the Finsbury Dispensary (1780).

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The London Dispensary opened its doors in 1696 as the first such clinic in the British Empire.

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: Dispensary
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A building or room for the distribution of medicines, eg. in a hospital or clinic.

types.name: Cottage hospital

period.text: which came first is argued: Wrington (1818), Piccotts End (1827, called the first), Wellow (1842) or Cranleigh (1859, the usual first); 294 founded 1855-98; still opening in 1940 (Leatherhead); now mostly called community hospitals

types.plan: a small rural building with a few beds, at most about 25

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Between 1855 and 1898, 294 cottage hospitals were established.

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1827 Sir Astley Cooper converted some cottages at Piccotts End, close to Hemel Hempstead, into the first cottage hospital providing free medical services.

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Sapte made a cottage available, rent-free, which after being whitewashed and simply furnished opened after a few weeks as the first cottage hospital.

sources.title: Leatherhead
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The cottage hospital on Poplar Road opened in May 1940 and by June of that year was treating 78 members of the British Expeditionary Force, who had been evacuated from Dunkirk.

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The term community hospital is now applied to most of these buildings where they are used to deliver healthcare, reflecting the wider range of services that are provided in more modern times.

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The original concept was a small rural building having several beds.

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: Cottage Hospital
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: Usually a rural hospital with up to 25 beds.

types.name: Royal naval hospital (Haslar, Stonehouse)

period.text: ordered in 1744; Haslar first received patients c. 1753, Stonehouse built 1758-65; smaller ones at Yarmouth (1793) and Deal (1800); the new hospital at Chatham of 1905 the latest; the last closed in 2009

types.plan: detached ward blocks (Stonehouse), foreshadowing the pavilion plan

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: One of the earliest pavilion hospitals in England is the Royal Naval Hospital, Stonehouse, near Plymouth, built from 1758.

sources.title: Royal Naval Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Royal Naval Hospital Haslar (Gosport); opened 1753 as the Royal Hospital Haslar, designated as the tri-Service core military hospital in 1996.

sources.title: Royal Naval Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Melville Hospital, Chatham: opened as a Royal Marine Infirmary in 1828, became a Royal Naval Hospital in 1885; replaced by a new Royal Naval Hospital in 1905

sources.title: Royal Naval Hospital, Stonehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Its pattern of detached wards (arranged so as to maximise ventilation and minimise spread of infection) foreshadowed the 'pavilion' style of hospital building which was popularised by Florence Nightingale a century later.

types.name: The Hôpital Lariboisière, Paris

period.text: built 1846-1853, opened 1854; one hospital, the model of the pavilion plan across Europe

types.plan: six buildings round a central courtyard, joined by colonnaded walkways (the double-comb layout)

sources.title: Lariboisière Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was built from 1846 to 1853 under architect Pierre Gauthier, with six buildings arranged around a central courtyard, connected by colonnaded walkways.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This organizational model spread mainly during the 19th century—notably with the construction in Paris of Lariboisière Hospital, opened in 1854—and reached its culmination in Lyon with Hôpital Édouard-Herriot, built by Tony Garnier between 1911 and 1933.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The most notable example of the double-comb type is the Lariboisière Hospital in Paris, inaugurated in 1854.

types.name: Pavilion-plan hospital

period.text: emerged in the 18th century (Stonehouse, from 1758); widespread in the 19th (the Royal Herbert Hospital, Woolwich, 1865); its last great example Lyon's Édouard-Herriot (1911-33); the block hospital took over from the 1930s

types.note: FISH has PAVILION WARD BLOCK (92870) for the ward blocks but no term for the hospital plan.
types.plan: separate ward pavilions, each joined to a central corridor for daylight and fresh air

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A pavilion hospital is a functional and spatial organization of hospitals that emerged in the 18th century and became widespread in the 19th century.

sources.title: Royal Herbert Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It utilised a new approach to open planning, and was based on the revolutionary 'pavilion' design whereby each ward was connected to a central corridor to maximise daylight and fresh air intake.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: One of the earliest pavilion hospitals in England is the Royal Naval Hospital, Stonehouse, near Plymouth, built from 1758.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This organizational model spread mainly during the 19th century—notably with the construction in Paris of Lariboisière Hospital, opened in 1854—and reached its culmination in Lyon with Hôpital Édouard-Herriot, built by Tony Garnier between 1911 and 1933.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From the 1930s onward, a new model, the block hospital, became dominant.

period.text: smallpox hospital 1741; fever hospitals from 1801; common after the notification Acts of 1889 and 1899 and the most common sort of hospital by 1914; wound down after the NHS began in 1948, few left by 1968

sources.title: Fever hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first hospital specifically for smallpox was the London Smallpox Hospital, founded in 1741.

sources.title: Fever hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first specialist hospital for other infectious diseases was the Liverpool Fever Hospital which was founded in 1801.

sources.title: Fever hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: As the germ theory of disease and nature of infection became established, more fever hospitals were established so that, by 1914, they were the most common sort of hospital.

sources.title: Fever hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: After the introduction of the National Health Service in 1948, the hospitals were wound down so that, by 1968, there were few left.

period.text: opened by Brehmer at Görbersdorf in 1854 in most accounts (1863 in the Sanatorium article); one institution, not a type built again

sources.title: Hermann Brehmer
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: a German physician who established the first German sanatorium for the systematic open-air treatment of tuberculosis

sources.title: Sokołowsko
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1854 she and Brehmer opened the world's first sanatorium for the treatment of tuberculosis at Görbersdorf.

sources.title: Sanatorium
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1863, Hermann Brehmer opened the Brehmersche Heilanstalt für Lungenkranke in Görbersdorf (Sokołowsko), Silesia (now Poland), for the treatment of tuberculosis.

period.text: Bodington's sanatorium at Sutton Coldfield (1836) or Brehmer's at Görbersdorf (1854) the first, as the accounts differ; common in Europe from the late 19th century; they began to close after streptomycin (1943), and no source here dates the last built

sources.title: Sanatorium
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first suggestion of sanatoria in the modern sense was likely made by George Bodington, who opened a sanatorium in Sutton Coldfield in 1836 and later published his essay "On the Treatment and Cure of Pulmonary Consumption" in 1840.

sources.title: Sanatorium
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Tuberculosis sanatoria became common throughout Europe from the late-19th century onward.

sources.title: Sanatorium
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: After 1943, when Albert Schatz, then a graduate student at Rutgers University, discovered streptomycin, an antibiotic and the first cure for tuberculosis, sanatoria began to close.

types.name: Workhouse infirmary
types.note: FISH INFIRMARY is used for the sick wards of a complex such as a workhouse.

period.text: small infirmary blocks in the union workhouses from the 1834 Act; separate infirmaries under their own management after 1867; the workhouse system ended in 1930, when councils could take the infirmaries over as municipal hospitals

types.plan: long corridors with separate wards for men, women and children (1840-75); later pavilions

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Most workhouses had a small infirmary block, but nursing was in the hands of the other inmates, most of whom could not read.

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The workhouse system was abolished in the UK by the same Act on 1 April 1930, but many workhouses, renamed Public Assistance Institutions, continued under the control of local county councils.

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These new buildings often had long corridors with separate wards leading off for men, women and children.

period.text: from the Local Government Act 1929 (few outside London); into the NHS in 1948

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: in 1929 legislation was passed to allow local authorities to take over workhouse infirmaries as municipal hospitals

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Local Government Act 1929 gave local authorities the power to take over workhouse infirmaries as municipal hospitals, although outside London few did so.

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The National Health Service, the principal provider of health care in Britain, was founded in 1948, and took control of nearly all the hospitals.

types.name: Almshouse (bede-house)

period.text: St Cross, Winchester (1136), called England's oldest almshouse; the word itself from the 14th century; many new foundations c. 1550-1650; still built, some 700-800 new homes a year in 2021

types.plan: medieval halls and courtyards, then from the late 16th century rows of cottages of one or two rooms each with its own fireplace

sources.title: Hospital of St Cross
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It has been described as "England's oldest and most perfect almshouse".

sources.title: Hospital of St Cross
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was founded by Henry of Blois, Bishop of Winchester, grandson of William the Conqueror and younger brother to King Stephen in 1136.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This pattern continued into the early modern period, with a marked increase in new foundations between about 1550 and 1650, particularly in towns, reflecting changing approaches to charity and poor relief.

sources.title: Inside Housing: Open alms: the almshouse charities building new homes
sources.author: The Almshouse Association
sources.quote: he estimates that almshouse charities are today building between 700 and 800 new homes a year, up from just a few hundred annually 20 years ago.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Residents were housed in separate rooms or small cottages, typically with one or two rooms and their own fireplace for heating and cooking.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the late 16th century, almshouses were commonly built as rows of cottages, usually located in the center of a village or town, near the parish church.

types.name: Royal hospital for old soldiers and seamen (Kilmainham, Chelsea, Greenwich)

period.text: Kilmainham, Dublin, built 1679-87, then Chelsea (founded 1682) and Greenwich (from 1692); Greenwich's Queen Mary Court, the last of the principal buildings, completed in 1742

types.plan: a formal front and a large enclosed courtyard, after Les Invalides (Kilmainham)

sources.title: Royal Hospital Chelsea
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: King Charles II founded the Royal Hospital as a retreat for veterans in 1682.

sources.title: Greenwich Hospital, London
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: She ordered the King Charles wing of the palace—originally designed by architect John Webb for King Charles II in 1664—to be remodelled as a naval hospital to provide a counterpart for the Chelsea Hospital for soldiers.

sources.title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The hospital was built as a home for retired soldiers of the Irish Army by Sir William Robinson, Surveyor General for James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, between 1679 and 1687 on what was then a portion of the Phoenix Park.

sources.title: Greenwich Hospital, London
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Queen Mary Court (planned by Wren and Hawksmoor, but not built until after Wren's death, by Thomas Ripley), completed in 1742

sources.title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The building was inspired by Les Invalides in Paris which also has a formal facade and a large enclosed courtyard.

types.name: Les Invalides, Paris

period.text: ordered by Louis XIV in 1670; the main complex complete in 1676 and the Dome chapel in 1706; one building, not a type built again

types.plan: a formal front and fifteen courtyards, the largest the cour d'honneur

sources.title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The building was inspired by Les Invalides in Paris which also has a formal facade and a large enclosed courtyard.

sources.title: Les Invalides
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Louis XIV initiated the project by an order dated 24 November 1670 to create a home and hospital for aged and disabled (invalide) soldiers, the veterans of his many military campaigns.

sources.title: Les Invalides
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Dome chapel was finished in 1706.

sources.title: Les Invalides
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the time the enlarged project was completed in 1676, the façade fronting the Seine measured 196 metres (643 ft) in width, and the complex had fifteen courtyards, the largest being the cour d'honneur designed for military parades.

types.name: Lunatic hospital (Bethlem and the charitable asylums)
types.note: FISH files every asylum under PSYCHIATRIC HOSPITAL.

period.text: insane patients at Bethlem by 1403; Bethlem rebuilt at Moorfields in 1676; charitable asylums from St Luke's (1751) to Liverpool (1797); Bethlem rebuilt again at St George's Fields in 1815, as the county asylums began

types.plan: cells off long galleries, men and women in separate wings (Bethlem, 1676 and 1815)

sources.title: Lunatic asylum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From the mid-eighteenth century the number of public charitably funded asylums expanded moderately with the opening of St Luke's Hospital in 1751 in Upper Moorfields, London

sources.title: Bethlem Royal Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The presence of a small number of insane patients in 1403 marks Bethlem's gradual transition from a diminutive general hospital into a specialist institution for the confinement of the insane.

sources.title: Lunatic asylum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1676, Bethlem expanded into newly built premises at Moorfields with a capacity for 100 inmates.

sources.title: Lunatic asylum
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the York Asylum in 1777 (not to be confused with the York Retreat); the Leicester Lunatic Asylum (1794), and the Liverpool Lunatic Asylum (1797).

sources.title: Bethlem Royal Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Bethlem rebuilt at St George's Fields"
sources.quote: Completed after three years in 1815, it was constructed during the first wave of county asylum building in England under the County Asylums Act 1808

sources.title: Bethlem Royal Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Bethlem rebuilt at St George's Fields"
sources.quote: Female patients occupied the west wing and males the east; as at Moorfields, the cells were located off galleries that traversed each wing.

types.name: County asylum (corridor plan)

period.text: after the County Asylums Act 1808; the first opened 1812 (Nottinghamshire); Hanwell (1831) copied widely; the corridor plan gave way to the echelon plan, first used successfully at Claybury (1893)

types.note: Hanwell (the First Middlesex County Asylum, 1831) had octagonal 'panopticon' towers at its centre and ends; the panopticon prison is a civic type and is not linked here.
types.plan: a corridor plan: long ward ranges joined by corridors (Wakefield, 1818)

sources.title: Psychiatric hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Nine counties first applied, the first public asylum opening in 1812 in Nottinghamshire.

sources.title: Claybury Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was the first asylum to successfully use the echelon plan upon which all later asylums were based.

sources.title: Stanley Royd Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The facility, which was designed by Watson and Pritchett using a corridor plan layout, was opened as the West Riding Pauper Lunatic Asylum in 1818.

period.text: Coney Hill, Gloucester (opened 1883), called the first built in true echelon plan though its outer sections were never built; Claybury (1893) the first to use it successfully, the model for all later asylums; Severalls (opened 1913) the latest found

sources.title: George Thomas Hine
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Hine was an early exponent of the 'echelon' design of asylums which he deployed at Claybury.

sources.title: Claybury Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was opened in 1893 making it the Fifth Middlesex County Asylum.

sources.title: Claybury Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was the first asylum to successfully use the echelon plan upon which all later asylums were based.

sources.title: Coney Hill Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was the first asylum to be built in true echelon plan.

sources.title: Coney Hill Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was designed by John Giles & Gough and opened as the Second Gloucestershire County Asylum in 1883.

sources.title: Coney Hill Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Outer sections to the echelon were planned but never implemented.

sources.title: Severalls Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The hospital was designed by Frank Whitmore, the county architect, and William Town using an echelon formation layout.

sources.title: Severalls Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The foundation stone was laid by Sir Thomas Barrett-Lennard in June 1910 and it opened as the Second Essex County Asylum in May 1913.

types.name: Parish workhouse

period.text: from 1631 (Abingdon); many after the Workhouse Test Act 1723, until the union workhouses of 1834

types.note: FISH WORKHOUSE covers both the parish and the union workhouse.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest known use of the term workhouse is from 1631, in an account by the mayor of Abingdon reporting that "we have erected within our borough a workhouse to set poorer people to work".

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This growth in the number of workhouses was prompted by the Workhouse Test Act 1723

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Individual parishes were grouped into Poor Law Unions, each of which was to have a union workhouse.

types.name: Union workhouse

period.text: after the Poor Law Amendment Act 1834: more than 500 built in the next 50 years, two-thirds of them by 1840; abolished 1930

types.note: Sampson Kempthorne's model plans of 1835 (square and Y or hexagonal) resembled Bentham's panopticon prison, and critics doubted that the likeness to model prisons was coincidental; the panopticon is a civic type and is not linked here.
types.plan: Kempthorne's model plans of 1835: a radial or octagonal centre in a walled yard, divided into yards for each class of inmate; from 1840 separate blocks linked by long corridors

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A common layout resembled Jeremy Bentham's prison panopticon, a radial design with four three-storey buildings at its centre set within a rectangular courtyard, the perimeter of which was defined by a three-storey entrance block and single-storey outbuildings, all enclosed by a wall.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Some critics of the new Poor Law noted the similarities between Kempthorne's plans and model prisons, and doubted that they were merely coincidental - Richard Oastler went as far as referring to the institutions as 'prisons for the poor'.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: More than 500 of these were built during the next 50 years, two-thirds of them by 1840.

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The workhouse system was abolished in the UK by the same Act on 1 April 1930, but many workhouses, renamed Public Assistance Institutions, continued under the control of local county councils.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: That basic layout, one of two designed by the architect Sampson Kempthorne (his other design was octagonal with a segmented interior, sometimes known as the Kempthorne star), allowed for four separate work and exercise yards, one for each class of inmate.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Typically the entrance building contained offices, while the main workhouse building housed the various wards and workrooms, all linked by long corridors designed to improve ventilation and lighting.

period.text: after the Poor Relief (Ireland) Act 1838: 130 unions, each with a workhouse designed by George Wilkinson; more unions were formed in the Famine (Portumna, 1850), the latest found

sources.title: Poor Relief (Ireland) Act 1838
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Following its enactment, one hundred and thirty Poor Law Unions were established throughout the country.

sources.title: Poor Relief (Ireland) Act 1838
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Each Union had a workhouse, financed by the payment of rates on landholders in the Union district.

sources.title: Portumna
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Portumna Union was formally declared on 22 February 1850, covering an area of 121 square miles (310 km2) as a subdivision of the Ballinasloe and Loughrea unions.

sources.title: Portumna
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Designed by the Poor Law Commissioners' architect George Wilkinson, the building was intended to accommodate 600 inmates who were badly affected by the lack of both employment and food at the time.

period.text: town poorhouses in the 18th century (Glasgow's Town's Hospital 1731, Edinburgh's Canongate 1761); most after the Poor Law (Scotland) Act 1845, fifty by 1868; the Poor Law ended in 1948

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Scottish poorhouse, occasionally referred to as a workhouse, provided accommodation for the destitute and poor in Scotland.

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By 1868 there were fifty poorhouses in Scotland; strict regulations applied to admissions and were overseen by a local Inspector of the Poor.

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In Aberdeen during the 1630s an institution had been established by wealthy cloth merchants; Canongate Charity Workhouse in Edinburgh was managed by several trade associations after being opened in 1761; and Glasgow had the Town's Hospital, opened in 1731.

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Expansions to existing facilities in Edinburgh and Glasgow and design guidelines for constructing new poorhouses were drawn up by the Board of Supervision which advised the parochial boards set up after the enactment of the Poor Law (Scotland) Act 1845.

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The number of inmates peaked in 1906 and after the introduction of the National Assistance Act 1948 (11 & 12 Geo. 6. c. 29), the Poor Law system was abolished throughout the United Kingdom.

types.name: Public baths

period.text: Liverpool 1828; under the Baths and Washhouses Act 1846, and by 1915 most towns in Britain had at least one; still built in 1961 (Bow Baths, with 60 slipper baths), the latest found, as homes gained bathrooms

types.note: Baths for washing, as a matter of hygiene; swimming baths and lidos are recreation types.

sources.title: Baths and wash houses in Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: salt-water baths were opened in 1828 by the Corporation of Liverpool

sources.title: Baths and wash houses in Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This was the first legislation to empower British local authorities to fund the building of public baths and wash houses.

sources.title: Public bathing
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The introduction of bath houses into British culture was a response to the public's desire for increased sanitary conditions, and by 1915 most towns in Britain had at least one.

sources.title: Roman Road, London
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1961, a new Bow Baths was built in Sutherland Place which included 60 slipper baths and a laundry block.

types.name: Public wash-house

period.text: Liverpool, 1842 (Frederick Street); still built with baths in 1961 (Bow Baths' laundry block), the latest found; demand fell as home laundry became easier

types.note: Kitty Wilkinson's washing of infected clothes in her own house in the cholera of 1832 is often called the first public wash-house; John Dobie (1972), from the council's records, showed the corporation's baths and wash-house opened in 1842, before the one she ran, and that her legend was built up later.

sources.title: Kitty Wilkinson
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Ten years later with public funds, her efforts resulted in the opening of a combined washhouse and public baths, the first in the United Kingdom.

sources.title: Kitty Wilkinson
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: A series of articles in 1972, published in Baths Service ‘The Journal of the Institute of Baths Management Incorporated’, argued that Kitty Wilkinson's life had become "a civic myth".

sources.title: Baths and wash houses in Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: George's Pier Head salt-water baths were opened in 1828 by the Corporation of Liverpool, with the first known warm fresh-water public wash house being opened in May 1842 on Frederick Street.

sources.title: Roman Road, London
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1961, a new Bow Baths was built in Sutherland Place which included 60 slipper baths and a laundry block.

sources.title: Stockton's public baths and wash house
sources.author: Stockton-on-Tees Borough Council heritage
sources.quote: As the development of domestic appliances made home laundry less onerous the demand for the wash-house declined, although the public laundry continued to be used for many years.

links.claim: Where the medieval hospital came from is argued: from the hospitals and guest houses that monasteries kept from the 10th century, or (Gordon) from houses first made to isolate lepers and plague victims and only later turned to serving pilgrims. In England most medieval hospitals were tied to the Church and many to monasteries.

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: During the 10th century, the monasteries became a dominant factor in hospital work.

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Benjamin Gordon supports the theory that the hospital – as we know it – is a French invention, but that it was originally developed for isolating lepers and plague victims, and only later undergoing modification to serve the pilgrim.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Most medieval hospitals in England were closely linked to the Church and often connected to monasteries, convents or other religious institutions.

views: Monastic: the monasteries' hospitals for pilgrims and the poor were the root of hospital work from the 10th century (History of hospitals, after the Catholic Encyclopedia).
Benjamin Gordon: the hospital was a French invention made first to isolate lepers and plague victims, and only later changed to serve pilgrims.

links.claim: The leper hospital is a medieval hospital founded for one purpose, the care of lepers, usually a church with separate shelters for them.

sources.title: Leper hospital (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 68717)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Some hospitals were multi-functional while others were founded for specific purposes such as leper hospitals, or as refuges for the poor, or for pilgrims: not all cared for the sick.

links.claim: The almshouse grew out of the medieval hospital: by the later Middle Ages it was a distinct, smaller house giving long-term homes to a settled group, mostly the old, rather than care to a passing population.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Almshouses developed from these earlier hospital foundations and were closely connected to both royal and religious authority.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the later medieval era, almshouses became more common, typically housing fewer residents than hospitals and focusing on long-term accommodation rather than care.

links.claim: As leprosy declined, some leper hospitals were turned into almshouses or other charitable housing.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: As leprosy declined, some former leprosy hospitals were adapted for use as almshouses or other forms of charitable housing.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Some institutions changed their role over time, and buildings originally founded for one purpose, such as leper hospitals, were later used to house other groups in need.

links.claim: The Royal Hospital at Chelsea (1682) was founded as an almshouse, in the old sense of 'hospital', for old soldiers; Greenwich was made its counterpart for seamen.

sources.title: Royal Hospital Chelsea
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Founded as an almshouse — the ancient sense of the word "hospital" —  by King Charles II in 1682

sources.title: Greenwich Hospital, London
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: She ordered the King Charles wing of the palace—originally designed by architect John Webb for King Charles II in 1664—to be remodelled as a naval hospital to provide a counterpart for the Chelsea Hospital for soldiers.

links.claim: Kilmainham was built after Les Invalides, with a formal front and a large closed courtyard, and Kilmainham and Les Invalides were together the model for Chelsea, where the idea of a hostel instead of pensions also came from Paris.

sources.title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The building was inspired by Les Invalides in Paris which also has a formal facade and a large enclosed courtyard.

sources.title: Royal Hospital Kilmainham
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Along with Les Invalides, it served as the model for the Royal Hospital, Chelsea, begun the next year under the guidance of Christopher Wren.

sources.title: Royal Hospital Chelsea
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The provision of a hostel rather than the payment of pensions was inspired by Les Invalides in Paris.

links.claim: Two medieval hospitals of London, St Bartholomew's and St Thomas's, were endowed again by the Crown after the Dissolution and are counted among the six voluntary hospitals of London by the mid-18th century; the voluntary hospital movement itself was one of new foundations from 1718. The sources give both; none says the new hospitals followed the old.

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: After the dissolution of the monasteries in 1540 by King Henry VIII the church abruptly ceased to be the supporter of hospitals, and only by direct petition from the citizens of London, were the hospitals St Bartholomew's, St Thomas's and St Mary of Bethlehem's (Bedlam) endowed directly by the crown.

sources.title: Voluntary hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By the middle of the 18th century, there were six in London: St Barts, Guy's, St Thomas', Westminster, St George's, and St Mary's (the last to be founded in England, in 1851).

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: From the mid-16th century until the Voluntary Hospital Movement in the early part of the 18th century there was a dearth of hospital care in the UK.

links.claim: Bethlem, founded in 1247 as a priory collecting alms, changed slowly from a small general hospital into a house for the insane, who are first recorded there in 1403; it was the first of the lunatic hospitals.

sources.title: Bethlem Royal Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The presence of a small number of insane patients in 1403 marks Bethlem's gradual transition from a diminutive general hospital into a specialist institution for the confinement of the insane.

sources.title: Bethlem Royal Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Bethlem was not initially intended as a hospital, in the clinical sense, much less as a specialist institution for the insane, but as a centre for the collection of alms to support the Crusader Church and to link England to the Holy Land.

links.claim: Bethlem's buildings at Moorfields (1676) and St George's Fields (1815) had cells off long galleries, and the early county asylums, built in the same years, were laid out on a corridor plan (Wakefield, 1818). The sources describe both; none says the county asylums copied Bethlem.

sources.title: Bethlem Royal Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Bethlem rebuilt at St George's Fields"
sources.quote: Female patients occupied the west wing and males the east; as at Moorfields, the cells were located off galleries that traversed each wing.

sources.title: Bethlem Royal Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Bethlem rebuilt at St George's Fields"
sources.quote: Completed after three years in 1815, it was constructed during the first wave of county asylum building in England under the County Asylums Act 1808

sources.title: Stanley Royd Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The facility, which was designed by Watson and Pritchett using a corridor plan layout, was opened as the West Riding Pauper Lunatic Asylum in 1818.

links.claim: The echelon plan grew out of the corridor asylum: Hanwell's plan was copied and modified for later asylums, Claybury among them, and Claybury (1893) was the first asylum to use the echelon plan successfully.

sources.title: St Bernard's Hospital, Hanwell
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Hanwell became a model for future hospitals and was copied and modified by the designers of countless other asylums across England and Wales (for example Horton, Colney Hatch, Claybury, or Springfield)

sources.title: Claybury Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was the first asylum to successfully use the echelon plan upon which all later asylums were based.

links.claim: Which was the first cottage hospital is argued, and with it whether the type began as a dispensary with a few beds: the thesaurus counts small dispensaries with in-patients from before Cranleigh (1859) as cottage hospitals, and Piccotts End (1827) is also called the first.

sources.title: Cottage hospital (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 91639)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: Usually a rural hospital with up to 25 beds. Can include small pre-Cranleigh institutions, eg: dispensaries with in-patients.

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Sapte made a cottage available, rent-free, which after being whitewashed and simply furnished opened after a few weeks as the first cottage hospital.

sources.title: Cottage hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1827 Sir Astley Cooper converted some cottages at Piccotts End, close to Hemel Hempstead, into the first cottage hospital providing free medical services.

views: Cranleigh: Albert Napper's village hospital in a cottage (1859) was the first cottage hospital, the reference point of the thesaurus ('pre-Cranleigh').

Earlier: small dispensaries with in-patients before Cranleigh count as cottage hospitals (the thesaurus), and Sir Astley Cooper's cottages at Piccotts End (1827) are called the first cottage hospital.

links.claim: The detached ward blocks of the Royal Naval Hospital at Stonehouse (1758-65) foreshadowed the pavilion plan; the French Academy's commission of 1786-88 took it as its reference model.

sources.title: Royal Naval Hospital, Stonehouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Its pattern of detached wards (arranged so as to maximise ventilation and minimise spread of infection) foreshadowed the 'pavilion' style of hospital building which was popularised by Florence Nightingale a century later.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This debate was ultimately settled by a commission of the French Academy of Sciences between 1786 and 1788, following study trips across Europe, during which the Stonehouse hospital was taken as the reference model.

links.claim: Lariboisière (opened 1854) carried the pavilion plan across Europe, and Florence Nightingale praised it in her Notes on Hospitals (with criticisms) while urging single-ward pavilions; the sources do not name a British hospital built after it.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: This organizational model spread mainly during the 19th century—notably with the construction in Paris of Lariboisière Hospital, opened in 1854

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Florence Nightingale and the Franco-British debate"
sources.quote: For example, Armand Husson (1809–1874), director of public assistance in 1859, extensively cited Nightingale's Notes on Hospitals when she praised Lariboisière Hospital, while omitting the criticisms she also expressed.

sources.title: Pavilion hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Florence Nightingale and the Franco-British debate"
sources.quote: Nightingale advocated ward-pavilions (single-ward pavilions), which she considered the healthiest form of hospital structure within the framework of aerist theories.

links.claim: Workhouse infirmaries grew from the workhouse's own sick wards, nursed by inmates, and after 1867 were separated from the workhouse under their own management.

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They developed from the Workhouse and were run under the Poor law regime.

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Most workhouses had a small infirmary block, but nursing was in the hands of the other inmates, most of whom could not read.

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The infirmary should be separated from the rest of the workhouse and under independent management

links.claim: By 1870 new workhouse buildings, the infirmaries among them, left the corridor plan for pavilions after the military hospitals of the Crimean War years (the Royal Herbert); Manchester's infirmary of 1878 had seven parallel pavilions.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: By 1870 the architectural fashion had moved away from the corridor design in favour of a pavilion style based on the military hospitals built during and after the Crimean War, providing light and well-ventilated accommodation.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Opened in 1878, the Manchester Union's infirmary comprised seven parallel three-storey pavilions

sources.title: Royal Herbert Hospital
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: the hospital quickly became a design figurehead for dozens more hospitals, both public and military

links.claim: From 1929 local authorities could take workhouse infirmaries over as municipal hospitals (few did outside London), and in 1948 the NHS took control of nearly all hospitals.

sources.title: Workhouse infirmary
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Local Government Act 1929 gave local authorities the power to take over workhouse infirmaries as municipal hospitals, although outside London few did so.

sources.title: History of hospitals
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The National Health Service, the principal provider of health care in Britain, was founded in 1948, and took control of nearly all the hospitals.

links.claim: In London after 1867 sick paupers with fevers and smallpox were to be moved out of the workhouses into separate hospitals, and the Metropolitan Asylums Board built smallpox and fever hospitals for them.

sources.title: Metropolitan Asylums Board
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Background to the establishment of the Metropolitan Asylums Board"
sources.quote: There was a particular concern that those suffering from infectious fevers and smallpox, and the insane, should be removed from the workhouses and treated in separate hospitals.

sources.title: Metropolitan Asylums Board
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "The first decades of Metropolitan Asylums Board"
sources.quote: The MAB purchased land and commenced building asylums at Leavesden in Hertfordshire and Caterham in Surrey, and smallpox and fever hospitals at Haverstock Hill in Hampstead, Homerton in East London and Stockwell in South London.

links.claim: The tuberculosis sanatorium is usually traced to Hermann Brehmer at Görbersdorf in Silesia (opened 1854, 1859 or 1863 in different accounts), but George Bodington opened a sanatorium at Sutton Coldfield in 1836. The sources do not say that a British sanatorium copied Görbersdorf; sanatoria became common across Europe from the late 19th century.

sources.title: Sokołowsko
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1854 she and Brehmer opened the world's first sanatorium for the treatment of tuberculosis at Görbersdorf.

sources.title: Sanatorium
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first suggestion of sanatoria in the modern sense was likely made by George Bodington, who opened a sanatorium in Sutton Coldfield in 1836 and later published his essay "On the Treatment and Cure of Pulmonary Consumption" in 1840.

sources.title: Sanatorium
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Tuberculosis sanatoria became common throughout Europe from the late-19th century onward.

views: From Görbersdorf: Brehmer's establishment of 1854 was the world's first sanatorium for tuberculosis (Sokołowsko).
English precursor: Bodington's sanatorium at Sutton Coldfield (1836) was likely the first suggestion of the sanatorium in the modern sense (Sanatorium).

links.claim: From the late 17th century the parish workhouse, paid for by the rates and open to all who qualified, took the place of new almshouses: after 1730 few almshouses were founded, as workhouses were thought cheaper.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Workhouses and the decline of almshouses"
sources.quote: Workhouses, introduced from the late 17th century, were parish-run institutions funded by local taxes to house the poor.

sources.title: Almshouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.locator: section "Workhouses and the decline of almshouses"
sources.quote: After 1730, new almshouse foundations declined, and some existing houses fell into neglect, as workhouses were increasingly favored as a more economical way to support larger numbers of people.

links.claim: The union workhouse grew from parishes sharing a workhouse: the Act of 1722 let parishes join to buy one, Gilbert's Act (1782) let them form unions for larger houses, and the Act of 1834 grouped every parish into a union with its own workhouse.

sources.title: Poor Relief Act 1722
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Where a parish could not afford to maintain a workhouse on their own, the act permitted the parish to join other parishes in purchasing a building for this purpose, so long as it had the permission of the vestry and a local Justice of the Peace.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Gilbert's Act was intended to allow parishes to share the cost of poor relief by joining together to form unions, known as Gilbert Unions, to build and maintain even larger workhouses to accommodate the elderly and infirm.

sources.title: Workhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Individual parishes were grouped into Poor Law Unions, each of which was to have a union workhouse.

links.claim: The Irish union workhouse is the English union workhouse carried to Ireland: the Act of 1838 was modelled on the English Act of 1834, each union had a workhouse, and the English workhouse architect George Wilkinson went to Ireland in 1839 as the Poor Law Commission's architect.

sources.title: Poor Relief (Ireland) Act 1838
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The legislation was largely influenced by the English Poor Law Amendment Act 1834.

sources.title: Poor Relief (Ireland) Act 1838
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Each Union had a workhouse, financed by the payment of rates on landholders in the Union district.

sources.title: George Wilkinson (architect)
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In 1839 George Wilkinson was invited to Ireland as the architect of the Poor Law Commission.

links.claim: The Scottish poorhouse is sometimes called a workhouse and, after 1845, parishes could combine to run one as English parishes formed unions; but the English reforms of 1834 did not apply in Scotland and its inmates were not usually set to work. The sources give the likeness and the separate laws; none calls it a convergence.

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The term poorhouse was almost invariably used to describe the institutions in that country, as unlike the regime in their workhouse counterparts in neighbouring England and Wales, residents were not usually required to labour in return for their upkeep.

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The 1707 Act of Union between Scotland and England had allowed Scotland to retain its existing legal system, so consequently the reforms to the Poor Law enacted in England and Wales in 1834 did not apply to Scotland.

sources.title: Scottish poorhouse
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The new law allowed parishes to combine to operate poorhouses jointly, the so-called combination poorhouses.

links.claim: The public wash-house is a laundry built with public baths; the first combined baths and wash-house opened in Liverpool in 1842.

sources.title: Public wash house (FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types, concept 87934)
sources.author: Historic England (Open Government Licence v3.0)
sources.quote: A laundry built in conjunction with a PUBLIC BATHS.

sources.title: Baths and wash houses in Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Wash houses often combined aspects of public bathing and self-service laundry.

sources.title: Kitty Wilkinson
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Ten years later with public funds, her efforts resulted in the opening of a combined washhouse and public baths, the first in the United Kingdom.
